title: Principles of Aquaculture
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Principles of Aquaculture curriculum: site selection, pond design/construction and types, culture systems (extensive, semi-intensive, intensive; monoculture, polyculture, integrated), major cultured species, water quality management, stocking and harvesting, hatchery/broodstock basics, and common aquaculture production systems used in Nigeria.

questions.question: Aquaculture is best defined as:
options: The farming of aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-controlled conditions
The random capture of wild fish from open water
The study of ocean tides
The processing of fish into canned products only
questions.correct_answer: The farming of aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-controlled conditions
questions.explanation: Aquaculture involves the deliberate cultivation of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, or aquatic plants under some degree of human management, distinguishing it from capture fisheries.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key factor to evaluate during site selection for a fish farm?
options: Availability of an adequate, reliable water supply of suitable quality
The presence of tall buildings nearby
Distance from any electricity supply
The number of birds in the area
questions.correct_answer: Availability of an adequate, reliable water supply of suitable quality
questions.explanation: A dependable water source of good quality and sufficient volume is one of the most critical requirements for successful fish farm siting.

questions.question: Soil type is an important site-selection consideration for earthen pond construction mainly because:
options: Clayey soil with good water-holding capacity minimizes seepage and maintains pond water levels
Sandy soil always holds water better than clay
Soil type has no effect on pond water retention
Rocky soil is ideal because it drains water rapidly
questions.correct_answer: Clayey soil with good water-holding capacity minimizes seepage and maintains pond water levels
questions.explanation: Soils with sufficient clay content reduce water seepage, helping earthen ponds retain water, whereas overly sandy or porous soils lead to excessive water loss.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an extensive aquaculture system?
options: A large earthen pond stocked at low density relying mainly on natural food with little to no supplementary feeding
A recirculating aquaculture system with computerized water quality control
A high-density cage system with complete artificial feed only
An indoor intensive tank system with continuous aeration
questions.correct_answer: A large earthen pond stocked at low density relying mainly on natural food with little to no supplementary feeding
questions.explanation: Extensive systems use low stocking densities and minimal inputs, depending largely on the pond's natural productivity to support fish growth.

questions.question: A semi-intensive aquaculture system is characterized by:
options: Moderate stocking density with some supplementary feeding and/or fertilization to boost natural productivity
Extremely low stocking density with zero inputs
The absence of any pond or containment structure
Complete reliance on natural food with no management inputs whatsoever
questions.correct_answer: Moderate stocking density with some supplementary feeding and/or fertilization to boost natural productivity
questions.explanation: Semi-intensive systems fall between extensive and intensive culture, using moderate stocking densities supplemented by feeding and/or pond fertilization to enhance yields.

questions.question: Intensive aquaculture systems are typically characterized by:
options: High stocking densities, complete artificial feed, and active water quality management (e.g. aeration)
Very low stocking densities with no management
Total reliance on natural pond productivity alone
The complete absence of any feeding regime
questions.correct_answer: High stocking densities, complete artificial feed, and active water quality management (e.g. aeration)
questions.explanation: Intensive systems maximize production per unit area/volume through high stocking density, complete nutritionally balanced feeds, and technologies like aeration or water exchange to sustain water quality.

questions.question: Polyculture in aquaculture refers to:
options: Rearing two or more compatible species together in the same water body to utilize different ecological niches
Growing a single fish species exclusively in one pond
Farming only plants with no animals involved
A system where no stocking occurs at all
questions.correct_answer: Rearing two or more compatible species together in the same water body to utilize different ecological niches
questions.explanation: Polyculture combines species with complementary feeding habits (e.g. surface feeders, bottom feeders, filter feeders) in one pond to maximize use of available food resources and space.

questions.question: Monoculture in aquaculture refers to:
options: Rearing a single fish species alone in a pond or culture unit
Rearing many different species together randomly
A system that combines crop farming and livestock only
The complete absence of stocking
questions.correct_answer: Rearing a single fish species alone in a pond or culture unit
questions.explanation: Monoculture involves culturing only one species at a time, simplifying management practices such as feeding and harvesting compared to polyculture.

questions.question: Integrated aquaculture (e.g. fish-cum-poultry or fish-cum-livestock farming) primarily aims to:
options: Utilize by-products or waste from one farming enterprise (e.g. animal manure) as nutrient input for fish ponds
Completely separate fish farming from any other agricultural activity
Eliminate the need for any fish feed whatsoever
Prevent the reuse of any farm resources
questions.correct_answer: Utilize by-products or waste from one farming enterprise (e.g. animal manure) as nutrient input for fish ponds
questions.explanation: Integrated systems combine aquaculture with crop or livestock farming so that waste products, such as poultry droppings, fertilize the pond and boost natural fish food production, improving overall farm efficiency.

questions.question: Which fish species is most widely cultured in Nigerian aquaculture due to its hardiness, fast growth, and tolerance of poor water quality?
options: African catfish (Clarias gariepinus)
Atlantic salmon
Rainbow trout
Common carp exclusively
questions.correct_answer: African catfish (Clarias gariepinus)
questions.explanation: Clarias gariepinus is the dominant cultured species in Nigeria because of its rapid growth, high tolerance of low dissolved oxygen, and strong market demand.

questions.question: Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) is a popular aquaculture species mainly because of its:
options: Fast growth, omnivorous feeding habit, and ease of breeding in captivity
Extremely slow growth rate
Requirement for very cold water temperatures
Inability to reproduce in captivity
questions.correct_answer: Fast growth, omnivorous feeding habit, and ease of breeding in captivity
questions.explanation: Nile tilapia is widely farmed worldwide, including Nigeria, due to its rapid growth, tolerance of varied conditions, omnivorous diet, and relative ease of reproduction and management.

questions.question: An earthen pond, as opposed to a concrete or plastic-lined tank, is typically favoured in Nigerian small-scale aquaculture mainly because it:
options: Is relatively cheaper to construct and supports natural food (plankton) production
Never requires any maintenance
Uses no water at all
Cannot support any fish species
questions.correct_answer: Is relatively cheaper to construct and supports natural food (plankton) production
questions.explanation: Earthen ponds are generally less costly to build than concrete structures and allow natural productivity (algae, plankton, benthic organisms) to develop, supplementing the fish diet.

questions.question: The 'dike' (or pond embankment) of an earthen fish pond primarily functions to:
options: Retain water within the pond and prevent flooding or seepage
Provide shade for the fish
Serve as the main source of fish feed
Filter incoming water
questions.correct_answer: Retain water within the pond and prevent flooding or seepage
questions.explanation: The dike, or embankment, forms the pond's walls, holding water in and protecting against external flooding, and must be well compacted to prevent seepage and collapse.

questions.question: A pond's 'monk' or outlet structure is designed to:
options: Control water level and allow controlled drainage/harvesting of the pond
Provide feed to the fish automatically
Aerate the water using solar power
Prevent any water from ever leaving the pond
questions.correct_answer: Control water level and allow controlled drainage/harvesting of the pond
questions.explanation: A monk (or similar outlet structure) allows the farmer to regulate water depth and facilitates complete or partial pond drainage, useful for harvesting.

questions.question: Fish ponds are commonly classified by function; a 'nursery pond' is specifically used for:
options: Rearing newly hatched fry to fingerling stage before stocking into grow-out ponds
Housing only broodstock fish for their entire lives
Storing harvested fish before sale
Growing only aquatic plants
questions.correct_answer: Rearing newly hatched fry to fingerling stage before stocking into grow-out ponds
questions.explanation: Nursery ponds provide a protected environment with appropriately sized food for vulnerable fry until they grow large enough (fingerlings) to be stocked into larger grow-out ponds.

questions.question: A 'grow-out' (production) pond is used primarily to:
options: Rear stocked fingerlings to marketable size
Hold broodstock exclusively for breeding purposes
Incubate fertilized fish eggs only
House only ornamental fish species
questions.correct_answer: Rear stocked fingerlings to marketable size
questions.explanation: Grow-out ponds are the main production units where fingerlings are cultured through to harvestable, marketable size.

questions.question: Fish cage culture involves:
options: Rearing fish in a mesh enclosure placed within a larger natural or man-made water body
Rearing fish exclusively in glass aquaria indoors
Growing fish entirely on dry land without water
A method used only for ornamental fish
questions.correct_answer: Rearing fish in a mesh enclosure placed within a larger natural or man-made water body
questions.explanation: Cage culture confines fish within a net or mesh cage suspended in an existing water body such as a lake, reservoir, or lagoon, allowing free water exchange through the mesh.

questions.question: A recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) is designed to:
options: Filter and reuse water continuously within a closed system, minimizing water use
Discharge all water after a single use with no filtration
Operate only in open natural water bodies
Avoid the use of any mechanical or biological filtration
questions.correct_answer: Filter and reuse water continuously within a closed system, minimizing water use
questions.explanation: RAS technology treats and recirculates culture water through mechanical and biological filters, greatly reducing water consumption compared to flow-through systems.

questions.question: In a recirculating aquaculture system, the biofilter's primary role is to:
options: Convert toxic ammonia into less harmful nitrite and then nitrate via nitrifying bacteria
Add oxygen to the water mechanically
Remove all dissolved minerals from the water
Heat the water to a constant temperature
questions.correct_answer: Convert toxic ammonia into less harmful nitrite and then nitrate via nitrifying bacteria
questions.explanation: The biofilter houses nitrifying bacteria that carry out biological nitrification, detoxifying ammonia excreted by fish into progressively less toxic nitrite and nitrate.

questions.question: Broodstock in aquaculture refers to:
options: Mature fish kept and managed specifically for breeding purposes to produce eggs and milt
Fish that have just been harvested for sale
Fingerlings ready for stocking into grow-out ponds
Fish that have died from disease
questions.correct_answer: Mature fish kept and managed specifically for breeding purposes to produce eggs and milt
questions.explanation: Broodstock are sexually mature, healthy fish selected and maintained under optimal conditions to produce quality eggs and sperm for hatchery propagation.

questions.question: In induced breeding of catfish, hormone injection (e.g. with ovaprim or pituitary extract) is used mainly to:
options: Stimulate final oocyte maturation and ovulation/spermiation in broodstock
Kill parasites on the fish's skin
Change the sex of the fish
Increase the fish's body length instantly
questions.correct_answer: Stimulate final oocyte maturation and ovulation/spermiation in broodstock
questions.explanation: Hormonal induction triggers the final stages of gamete maturation and release, allowing hatchery operators to strip eggs and milt for artificial fertilization at a controlled time.

questions.question: 'Stripping' in catfish hatchery operations refers to:
options: Manually applying gentle pressure to the abdomen of ripe broodstock to release eggs or milt
Removing scales from the fish's body
Cutting the fish's fins for identification
Weighing the fish before sale
questions.correct_answer: Manually applying gentle pressure to the abdomen of ripe broodstock to release eggs or milt
questions.explanation: Stripping is the manual expression of eggs from females or milt from males once they are fully ripe, typically after hormonal induction, for use in artificial fertilization.

questions.question: Stocking density in a fish pond refers to:
options: The number (or biomass) of fish stocked per unit area or volume of water
The number of fish species present in the pond
The total feed given to the pond per day
The depth of the pond in metres
questions.correct_answer: The number (or biomass) of fish stocked per unit area or volume of water
questions.explanation: Stocking density describes how many fish (or how much fish biomass) are placed in a given pond area or volume, a key factor influencing growth rate and management needs.

questions.question: Excessively high stocking density in a fish pond without corresponding increases in feeding and aeration typically leads to:
options: Poor water quality, stunted growth, and increased disease/mortality risk
Automatically faster growth for all fish
Improved water clarity
No change in fish health or growth
questions.correct_answer: Poor water quality, stunted growth, and increased disease/mortality risk
questions.explanation: Overstocking increases competition for oxygen and food and raises waste output, which can degrade water quality and lead to slower growth, stress, and higher disease incidence.

questions.question: 'Partial harvesting' in fish culture refers to:
options: Removing only the larger, marketable fish while leaving smaller ones to continue growing
Draining the entire pond and removing all fish at once
Harvesting fish from only one species in a polyculture system
Discarding all fish without selling any
questions.correct_answer: Removing only the larger, marketable fish while leaving smaller ones to continue growing
questions.explanation: Partial harvesting selectively removes fish that have reached market size, reducing density for the remaining stock and allowing continued growth and staggered marketing.

questions.question: Pond fertilization with organic manure or inorganic fertilizer in extensive/semi-intensive aquaculture aims primarily to:
options: Stimulate the growth of natural food organisms such as phytoplankton and zooplankton
Directly increase the fish's body weight without any biological process
Sterilize the pond water completely
Reduce the pond's water level
questions.correct_answer: Stimulate the growth of natural food organisms such as phytoplankton and zooplankton
questions.explanation: Fertilization adds nutrients that boost primary productivity (phytoplankton growth), which in turn supports zooplankton and other natural food organisms that fish can consume.

questions.question: Liming of fish ponds, typically with agricultural lime, is a common pre-stocking practice used to:
options: Neutralize soil/water acidity and help eradicate unwanted organisms
Increase the pond's water acidity dramatically
Remove all dissolved oxygen from the water
Permanently colour the water black
questions.correct_answer: Neutralize soil/water acidity and help eradicate unwanted organisms
questions.explanation: Liming raises pH in acidic pond soils/water, improves nutrient availability, and helps control pathogens and predatory organisms before stocking.

questions.question: Dissolved oxygen depletion is one of the most critical water quality concerns in intensive fish culture because it can lead to:
options: Stress, reduced feeding, and potentially mass fish mortality
Immediate improvement in fish growth
An increase in water clarity only
No significant impact on fish health
questions.correct_answer: Stress, reduced feeding, and potentially mass fish mortality
questions.explanation: Fish require adequate dissolved oxygen for respiration; low oxygen levels cause stress, appetite loss, and can result in mass mortality if not corrected promptly, especially at high stocking densities.

questions.question: Ammonia toxicity in fish ponds is primarily caused by:
options: Accumulation of fish excretory waste and decomposing uneaten feed/organic matter
Excessive dissolved oxygen in the water
Complete absence of any fish in the pond
Overuse of agricultural lime
questions.correct_answer: Accumulation of fish excretory waste and decomposing uneaten feed/organic matter
questions.explanation: Ammonia builds up mainly from fish metabolic waste (gill excretion) and the breakdown of excess feed and organic matter, becoming toxic at elevated concentrations, especially at high pH.

questions.question: Aeration devices (e.g. paddlewheel aerators) are used in intensive fish ponds mainly to:
options: Increase dissolved oxygen levels and improve water circulation
Reduce the pond's total water volume
Eliminate the need for any water quality monitoring
Increase ammonia concentration intentionally
questions.correct_answer: Increase dissolved oxygen levels and improve water circulation
questions.explanation: Aerators mechanically introduce atmospheric oxygen into water and promote mixing, preventing oxygen depletion, especially critical in high-density or nighttime low-oxygen conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'carrying capacity' as applied to an aquaculture pond?
options: The maximum fish biomass the pond can sustainably support given its water quality and management inputs
The total volume of water the pond can hold
The number of workers needed to manage the pond
The market price of fish produced from the pond
questions.correct_answer: The maximum fish biomass the pond can sustainably support given its water quality and management inputs
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity in aquaculture reflects the upper limit of fish biomass a given system can support without water quality or health problems, influenced by aeration, feeding, and management.
